text: FlowValue AI — Industry-Standard Product Development Roadmap
Engineering, AI, techno-economic modelling, validation and industrial adoption | Proposed roadmap, November 2026
I recommend converting the 14 recommendations into 10 structured development phases, supported by measurable milestones, testing protocols and mandatory acceptance gates.
The intention is to transform FlowValue from its existing development-stage platform into a validated engineering and techno-economic assessment system suitable for professional industrial use.

This roadmap builds on FlowValue’s existing architecture rather than replacing it. It retains the established Python calculation engines, AI-assisted workflows, MECE Revenue Box, equipment-costing systems, financial modelling, source records and project-version controls.
Each phase should produce three outcomes: a working capability, documented evidence that it works, and a clear decision on whether it is ready for the next stage.
Phase 0 — Baseline audit and product requirements
Phase 3 — Equipment design, costing and CAPEX
Phase 4 — OPEX, Revenue Box and financial modelling
Phase 5 — AI engineering intelligence and review
Phase 6 — Simulator interoperability and design visualisation
Phase 7 — Uncertainty, benchmarking and professional outputs
Phase 9 — Independent industrial validation and commercial adoption

The sequence describes the order of acceptance gates, not a requirement to develop everything sequentially. For example, security engineering, test automation, and external validation planning should begin in Phase 0 and continue throughout development.
2. How the 14 recommendations map to the phases
Phase 0 — Baseline audit, requirements and development controls
Objective: Establish exactly what FlowValue currently does, what remains incomplete, and how every future development claim will be validated.
Audit the existing backend, frontend, API, calculation modules, source ingestion and data-storage components.
Build a capability register classifying every feature as implemented, partially implemented, planned, unverified or deprecated.
Identify duplicate calculations, inconsistent data contracts, unsupported costing models and disconnected modules.
Document the existing engineering and financial data flow.
Establish a single, version-controlled requirements and acceptance register.
Create a continuous integration pipeline that checks the backend, frontend, APIs and calculation modules on every proposed code change.
Define standard rules for numerical precision, engineering units, missing data, evidence provenance, approvals and exceptions.
Establish an independent test-reference policy so project workbooks are not used to validate themselves.
Reproduce the current application from a clean development environment.
Confirm that every supported application module loads and passes its existing tests.
Record baseline failures rather than suppressing them.
Confirm that saved project revisions can be reopened without modifying the original baseline.
Confirm that the test environment does not disclose credentials or confidential project data.
Verify that every planned feature has an accountable owner and a measurable acceptance criterion.
EXIT GATE — G0: The baseline can be reproduced, existing failures are documented, critical security issues are triaged, and implementation status is distinguishable from roadmap promises.
Phase 1 — Engineering calculation engine and independent verification
Objective: Ensure that FlowValue’s numerical calculations are accurate, reproducible, physically appropriate and independently verifiable.
Create a central calculation-method registry that contains the method identifier, governing equations, required inputs, units, applicability range, source, version and error behaviour.
Standardise numerical treatment across equipment sizing, unit conversions, costing, CAPEX, OPEX, revenue and finance.
Introduce strong dimensional validation so incompatible units cannot silently produce a result.
For example, equipment sizing calculations must distinguish mass flow from volumetric flow, gauge pressure from absolute pressure, and purchased equipment cost from installed equipment cost.
Implement a formal error-handling framework with distinct states for missing inputs, invalid inputs, unsupported methods, extrapolated results and completed calculations.
Keep the deterministic Python calculation engine independent of AI-generated numerical answers.
Independent reference cases for each supported method
Unit tests: Compare each method against independently calculated examples.
Dimensional tests: Reject incompatible units and ambiguous measurement bases.
Boundary tests: Check zero, negative, missing, extreme and out-of-range inputs.
Regression tests: Verify that software changes do not alter previously correct calculations unexpectedly.
Reproducibility tests: Confirm that identical inputs, methods and software versions produce identical outputs.
100% of production-supported calculation methods have an identified verification reference and applicability statement.
No unsupported calculation is silently treated as valid.
All critical reported results can be traced to their inputs and method versions.
Numerical tolerances are defined independently for each method; one arbitrary percentage is not applied to every calculation.
EXIT GATE — G1: An independent reviewer can reproduce every designated critical reference calculation and identify its validity limits.
Objective: Establish one reliable engineering project model connecting every technical and economic module.
Create a canonical project schema representing:
Commercial contracts, revenue and avoided costs.
Implement unique identifiers and relationships so each physical asset is counted only once, even when the workbook contains multiple names or aliases.
Create a dependency graph allowing FlowValue to identify which results require recalculation after changes.

For instance, changing an inlet flow should trigger applicable equipment-sizing and cost calculations, but it should not automatically overwrite approved equipment arrangements or fixed commercial reservations.
Use at least three structurally different M&E workbooks and one manually defined process.
Test repeated equipment tags, missing stream properties, conflicting units, inconsistent operating schedules and changes to approved assumptions.
Perform controlled input mutations and independently calculate expected downstream changes.
Also test failed migrations and recovery of historical assessments.
Every critical engineering and commercial quantity has a documented source or assumption.
Approved assumptions are never silently overwritten.
Missing values remain distinguishable from zero.
Original workbooks remain unchanged after ingestion.
Existing saved projects survive schema migrations or receive a documented conversion route.
EXIT GATE — G2: One approved engineering change propagates correctly across the canonical project model without creating duplicate assets, stale results or hidden assumptions.
Phase 3 — Equipment design, costing and AACE-aligned capital estimation
Objective: Develop a reliable industrial equipment and capital-estimating system that explicitly reports its scope and estimate maturity.

Equipment engineering: Expand the validated method library for selected equipment families, prioritising pumps, heat exchangers, storage vessels, reactors, compressors, separation equipment and utilities.

Cost correlations: Support documented, appropriately licensed cost correlations, purchased-versus-installed scopes, material factors, pressure factors, dated escalation, currency conversion and approved vendor quotations.

Scope completeness: Build a plant capital breakdown that considers equipment, installation, piping, instrumentation, electrical infrastructure, civil works, utilities, buildings, engineering, construction management, commissioning and owner costs.

Estimate maturity: Implement an AACE-aligned estimate-class assessment that considers the maturity of project definition and identifies missing deliverables. The software should propose the classification for review, not certify it automatically.
Uncertainty: Tie cost ranges to the actual estimate maturity, available quotations and applicable statistical or engineering evidence.
Use independently established equipment cases to compare purchased and installed costs, factors and escalation.
Run deliberate duplicate-tag tests, missing-equipment tests, historical cost-year tests and installed-versus-purchased boundary tests.
Test the capital breakdown against a reference project with independently established scope.
Critically, verify that adding installation costs does not double-count installation already embedded in a costing methodology.
All priority equipment models have independently tested calculations.
All material costing sources have valid scope, year, currency and method information.
The reference plant achieves the agreed equipment-pricing coverage target, provisionally 95% of verified equipment scope.
Every unpriced item is visible, with its potential significance assessed.
The reported estimate class is consistent with documented design maturity.
The Basis of Estimate identifies scope, exclusions, assumptions and uncertainty.
EXIT GATE — G3: FlowValue produces an independently reviewable preliminary plant capital estimate without concealing missing equipment or double-counting installed costs.
Phase 4 — Integrated OPEX, Revenue Box and financial modelling
Objective: Create a fully connected economic model where engineering operations, operating expenditure, commercial payments and financial results remain consistent across all project years.
Operating expenditure: Develop a comprehensive operating cost ledger covering feedstocks, utilities, labour, maintenance, consumables, waste management, insurance, laboratory testing and overheads.
Each expense should have a clearly defined quantity, rate, escalation basis, payment owner, schedule and fixed/variable classification.
Revenue Box: Retain FlowValue’s existing six MECE revenue categories and enforce their commercial rules.

Every revenue source must preserve your established 13-field structure, including the payment mechanism, workbook quantity source, billable units, payment conditions, operating years and missing inputs.
Avoided costs: Develop a counterfactual-cost framework that distinguishes operational savings from customer payments and reduces the appropriate existing OPEX line without counting the benefit twice.
Financial modelling: Connect CAPEX, OPEX and revenue to project and equity cash flows, depreciation, taxation, debt, working capital, NPV, IRR, payback and relevant levelised-cost metrics.
Fully source-linked fixed and variable OPEX ledger
Revenue Box commercial-authority and payment-validation system
Reconciled financial workbook and reporting outputs
Use your wastewater treatment project as one internal integration fixture.
Verify that the system distinguishes the following independently:
Then change one assumption at a time and verify the expected effect.
For example, increasing treated wastewater volume should update volume-based service revenue while leaving a separately contracted fixed capacity reservation unchanged.
Test contract expiry in 2027, renewal in 2028, partial-year operations, zero production, unsold products and conflicting billing units.
No revenue source exists without explicit Revenue Box authority or an approved user edit.
Every commercial payment is uniquely identified.
Different payments using the same physical stream are reviewed for double-counting.
Contracts do not extend beyond their supported dates without an explicit assumption.
Avoided costs cannot be recognised as both OPEX savings and independent revenue without a separate valid payment mechanism.
Python, financial exports and dashboard values reconcile within defined numerical tolerances.
EXIT GATE — G4: FlowValue can produce a complete, reproducible multi-year financial model for a supported reference project, with commercial assumptions and financial calculations fully traceable.
Phase 5 — AI engineering intelligence and controlled professional review
Objective: Develop AI capabilities that support engineering reasoning, identify missing information and coordinate multidisciplinary analysis without compromising numerical reliability.
Develop a coordinated specialist architecture for process engineering, equipment design, equipment costing, operations, revenue strategy, financial interpretation and engineering review.
Each specialist should operate using restricted tools, validated schemas and defined authority boundaries.
The process engineering specialist should identify streams, equipment, assumptions and inconsistencies.
The equipment specialist should identify supported sizing methods and highlight missing or unsuitable data.
The cost specialist should propose applicable costing methods, never inventing a source-backed price.
The commercial specialist should interpret only authorised revenue mechanisms and generate reviewable assumptions.
The engineering review specialist should independently inspect the proposed analysis for contradictions, missing scope and unsupported decisions.
Introduce an approval workflow where engineer acceptance is tied to the exact assumption value, source basis and project version.
Specialist AI architecture with defined responsibilities
AI decision provenance and reproducible audit logs
Ask for the required design input or retain unresolved status
Preserve the missing price rather than inventing one
Prevent duplicate costing until identity is resolved
Preserve project data and allow deterministic operations to continue
Attempted instruction injection in an uploaded file
Treat file content as data, not executable instructions
Use a fixed evaluation suite across AI model and prompt updates. Measure source attribution, grounded accuracy, unsupported numerical claims, critical omission rates and approval-boundary violations.
No AI-generated calculation formula executes outside the approved deterministic method library.
All consequential AI-proposed assumptions are reviewable before application.
No autonomous modification of approved project baselines.
Zero critical approval-bypass failures in the release evaluation suite.
Zero accepted fabricated source citations in the release evaluation suite.
Documented thresholds for noncritical errors, reviewed by engineering subject-matter experts.
EXIT GATE — G5: AI can reliably assist with supported engineering and commercial workflows while preserving reviewer authority, calculation integrity and source traceability.
Phase 6 — Simulator interoperability and engineering visualisation
Objective: Allow FlowValue to work alongside established engineering software and interpret engineering information supplied in different formats.
Build versioned adapters for Excel/CSV, DWSIM exports, Aspen-compatible exported reports and structured engineering data.
Each adapter should preserve source units, stream names, property bases, equipment identifiers and provenance.
Develop an import preview showing mapped and unmapped data before accepting it into the canonical project model.
For process visualisation, distinguish between physical connectivity proven by imported data and schematic connections merely proposed by the system.
Introduce connected 2D process diagrams and progressively enhance 3D representations where reliable geometric information is available.
Do not automatically describe schematic or AI-generated representations as verified engineering drawings.
Validated Excel and CSV import library
Test each adapter against independently prepared files containing complex compositions, alternate units, nonstandard equipment tags and missing fields.
Check mass and energy balance consistency after import.
Verify that converting temperatures, pressures and flow rates preserves the correct physical quantities.
Compare imported results with the original engineering export.
Test false connectivity to ensure FlowValue never invents piping or material paths that are unsupported by the source.
100% of supported adapter test fixtures import and reconcile as specified.
Unmapped fields and unsupported source versions are disclosed.
No source data is silently altered or assigned an incorrect physical meaning.
Process diagrams distinguish verified connectivity from inferred or illustrative connectivity.
Users can reproduce an imported design basis from the original files.
EXIT GATE — G6: FlowValue reliably imports and interprets engineering data from its declared supported formats without losing critical information or fabricating process connections.
Phase 7 — Advanced uncertainty, benchmarking and professional deliverables
Primary focus: Recommendation 9 and analytical completeness
Objective: Make FlowValue capable of producing defensible risk assessments and professional-quality engineering investment reports.
Expand scenario analysis into an auditable uncertainty framework.
Support justified input distributions, correlated variables, constrained scenarios, stochastic calculations and sensitivity analysis.
Uncertainty distributions must be based on evidence or clearly identified assumptions. A nominal ±20% range should never be treated as a calibrated probability distribution without justification.
Build independent numerical benchmarks for equipment costing, OPEX, revenue, depreciation, financial metrics and Monte Carlo calculations.

Create a unified reporting pipeline that generates a technical report, editable financial workbook, project-assumptions register, financial dashboards and presentation material from the same approved study revision.
Introduce visible estimate-completeness indicators, including critical missing items and their impact on the confidence of economic results.
Monte Carlo sampling and dependence controls
Run reproducibility tests using fixed random seeds.
Compare Monte Carlo summary statistics with independently implemented statistical references.
Check that invalid samples, missing costs and incomplete equipment scope cannot silently contribute to claims about complete-project financial risk.
Confirm that every output uses the same cost basis, project year and operating schedule.
Perform dashboard, API, Excel and PDF reconciliation tests for the same approved assessment.
Repeated seeded uncertainty studies produce matching results within documented numerical tolerances.
Input distributions and correlations are fully documented.
Financial risk indicators are withheld or qualified when the underlying cost scope is incomplete.
All published project financial results reconcile across formats.
Every report discloses model limitations, uncertainty assumptions and unresolved material risks.
EXIT GATE — G7: FlowValue can deliver a professionally reviewable investment study with independently checked numerical results, transparent uncertainty and consistent reporting.
Phase 8 — Enterprise reliability, collaboration and security
Objective: Make FlowValue safe and reliable enough for industrial organisations to use with confidential engineering and financial information.
Develop an enterprise project workspace with defined access permissions, team collaboration, project ownership, engineering approvals and version-controlled assessment records.
Strengthen the existing cloud infrastructure with robust authentication, tenant isolation, secret management, backup and recovery, monitoring, logging and deployment controls.
Separate development, testing and production environments.
Implement asynchronous job infrastructure for computationally demanding studies, including recoverable execution states, cancellation and job-history records.
Build a documented service architecture covering system availability, database integrity, engineering calculation integrity and operational incidents.

Establish security and AI governance processes using applicable standards such as ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 42001 and NIST guidance as reference frameworks. Formal conformity or certification would require separate assessment.
Perform automated and manual security assessments covering authentication, authorisation, cross-tenant access, malicious uploads, sensitive-data exposure and API security.
Test simultaneous project edits to ensure that conflicting revisions cannot silently overwrite one another.
Simulate backend failures, interrupted Monte Carlo studies, database unavailability and incomplete uploads.
Carry out backup restoration exercises and verify that the restored project retains its approved inputs, source records, method versions and calculation outputs.
Zero unresolved critical security vulnerabilities at release.
All cross-tenant access isolation tests pass.
Project approval and revision histories remain consistent under concurrent edits.
Interrupted calculations have a documented recovery or safe-restart mechanism.
Backup restoration passes defined recovery-point and recovery-time objectives.
Enterprise operational controls are documented and independently reviewed where appropriate.
EXIT GATE — G8: FlowValue satisfies the security, reliability and collaboration requirements agreed for its first industrial deployments.
Phase 9 — Industrial validation, professional recognition and commercial adoption
Objective: Demonstrate that FlowValue delivers measurable value and reliable results in practical engineering environments.
Proposed planning window: Months 15–36 and continuing thereafter.
Select independent industrial partners across supported engineering sectors.
I would begin with three practical use cases:
A chemical or energy process-development project.
A water or wastewater treatment facility.
A bioprocess or emerging industrial technology project.
For each pilot, define the expected project scope, engineering inputs, required calculations, independent comparison method and intended decision.
Have practising engineers carry out structured comparisons between FlowValue and existing TEA workflows.
Measure not just numerical agreement but also workflow efficiency, engineering completeness, traceability and required manual intervention.
Submit identified defects and limitations to a controlled improvement process, then repeat the relevant validation tests.
Investigate professional recognition and collaboration opportunities with bodies such as IChemE and AACE, without assuming that a software accreditation route exists.
Three completed, independently assessed pilot studies
Established customer support and maintenance programme
Documented professional recognition or independent assurance pathway
For each pilot, evaluate the following independently:
All material scope and exclusions identified
Methods suitable for actual process conditions
Study completion time against the existing workflow
Independent engineer can reproduce the study
Practising engineers can complete defined tasks without developer assistance
At least three independently reviewed industrial pilots are completed.
Every critical pilot finding is resolved or explicitly retained as a limitation of the supported scope.
Customer engineering reviewers approve the software for their specified use cases.
There is evidence of repeatable value, rather than reliance on one successful demonstration.
No unsupported institutional accreditation or certification claims are made.
EXIT GATE — G9: FlowValue demonstrates credible engineering accuracy, practical usability and repeatable value within a clearly specified industrial scope.
The timeline below is a proposed planning baseline. It is not a delivery commitment; staffing, technical dependencies, development complexity and validation findings may change the schedule.
Overlapping phases indicate parallel development. Phase completion is determined by the acceptance gate, not the planned end date.
I would organise development into four externally meaningful releases rather than market every development phase as a new product.
Reproducible engineering foundation and reliable internal calculation workflows
Supported engineering-economic assessments with controlled AI review
External pilot studies, supported imports and professional reports
Demonstrated industrial use, security assurance and independent review within a declared scope
An industrial release should not be claimed simply because development has reached month 18 or 36.
These metrics should be monitored continuously. The targets are proposed release criteria, not current performance claims.
≥95% of verified reference-plant scope, with justified methods
At least 3 before claiming broader industrial readiness
Proposed targets. These bars illustrate required thresholds, not measured progress.
All required critical reference tests pass.
Critical outputs retain source and method provenance.
Physical equipment scope priced with justified methods; residual materiality still reviewed.
Supported API, dashboard and export reference cases reconcile.
No unresolved critical security findings at release.
At least three externally reviewed project studies.

Quality gates should also include explicit severity thresholds. A critical defect that can materially alter project value, corrupt engineering data, misrepresent a cost estimate or bypass an approval should block the applicable release, regardless of the total number of passing tests.
To make this operational, I recommend creating one GitHub milestone per development phase, with issues organised into the following work types.
Design specification, interfaces, dependencies and migration considerations
Exact functional behaviour and affected components
Reference methodology, independent expected values and numerical tolerances
Threat or failure scenario, test and required mitigation
Technical evidence, limitations and usage guidance
Completed test evidence, unresolved findings and approval decision
Each development issue should contain a clear problem statement, planned deliverable, implementation constraints, dependencies, test cases and evidence required for closure.
A milestone should not be considered complete because all coding tasks are marked done. It should close only when its acceptance gate is passed.
Example: A complete Phase 4 development ticket
FV-ECON-004 — Multi-year Revenue Box contract validation
Objective: Ensure that commercial payments cannot be recognised outside their authorised contractual period without an explicit approved assumption.
Implementation scope: Introduce effective and expiry dates, renewal terms, operating-year reconciliation, billable annual quantities and corresponding revenue scheduling.
Test scenario: A wastewater treatment agreement applies to 2027, while the project operates in 2027 and 2028.

Expected behaviour: FlowValue calculates the 2027 arrangement, flags 2028 as unresolved, and requests an explicit renewal or replacement contract assumption before recognising corresponding 2028 income.
☐ A 2027-only agreement does not automatically create 2028 revenue.
☐ An approved renewal creates the correct 2028 schedule.
☐ Billing units and quantities reconcile to the approved operating schedule.
☐ Editing the agreement does not overwrite the earlier approved version.
☐ Financial outputs and exported workbooks match the approved schedule.

The scope is substantial, so I would divide ownership into five technical responsibilities: process-engineering methods, backend/data architecture, AI and research workflows, frontend/product design, and quality/security engineering.
External practising engineers should participate in milestone reviews from the beginning, particularly for equipment design, capital costing, safety-relevant assumptions and industrial pilots.
A small team can combine roles initially. However, the person who implements a critical engineering calculation should not be its only validator.
Maintain a standing technical review board, even if initially only a few people, to approve method additions, critical model changes, acceptance criteria and releases.
Despite the scale of the roadmap, I would avoid starting ten major development streams simultaneously.
For FlowValue’s next development cycle, I would focus on achieving G0, G1 and the core of G2.

That means first knowing exactly what the current system supports, independently verifying the existing calculations, making the engineering data model reliable and establishing the test framework that all subsequent features will use.
Once those foundations are demonstrated, equipment costing and integrated TEA development should become the central delivery priority.
The first product target should be an independently validated, end-to-end preliminary techno-economic assessment for one defined industrial process.
From there, expand the supported domain systematically, rather than assuming one successful workbook proves universal engineering applicability.

The roadmap’s ultimate success criterion is straightforward: an industrial engineer should be able to use FlowValue to create a study, inspect every important assumption, reproduce its calculations, understand its limitations, and confidently defend the assessment during a technical or investment review.
That is the standard I would use to guide FlowValue’s development toward industry adoption.
